title: The Witch, The Dragon, and The Missing Pebble
markdown:
Witch Brindle adjusted her spectacles. Moonlight ran along jars of dried moonpetal and powdered grumbleweed, each label facing the same way. Her cottage sat on a high ledge over Whispering Valley, a small orderly island in a sea of pines. Outside, the wind sang through ancient trees. Pepper, a sleek black cat with emerald eyes, twitched a velvet ear from the warmest hearthstone and went on being a furry sentinel of domestic peace. The hearth hummed. The herbs smelled of last summer. Brindle liked a world that stayed where she had put it.

A flutter of parchment landed on the doorstep, tied with gossamer that looked as if it had borrowed starlight. The Elder Council’s script was hurried and spidery. An important parcel — the recalibrated heartstone for the annual Sunstone Festival — had to reach the Wise Hermit on the highest peak before the moon hit its zenith. If it did not, the festival would be cancelled, and the valley would spend a week in gloomy silence.

Brindle’s fingers paused on a particularly interesting moss by the lintel. She could have spent an hour on the angle of a spider’s web. The parcel would not wait for moss. She secured it in a reinforced leather satchel and checked the buckles twice.

“Well, Pepper. Off we go, whether we planned it or not.”

Pepper stretched, tail high, and trotted to the door. Brindle gave her shelves a last glance — a silent promise to return them to peace — pulled her woolen shawl tight, and stepped into pine-sharp air.

The descent toward the valley floor brought the rope bridges: each one swaying like a nervous dancer. Frost patterned the pines. Unusual fungi clustered on the shadowed sides of rocks. Brindle placed one worn boot carefully in front of the other. One bridge was slick with mist, its planks groaning. The chasm below was a silent drop. She did not look down for long.

A shadow fell over them, vast and impossibly grand. A dragon landed with a thud that shook pinecones loose. His scales were a thousand polished emeralds.

“Greetings, diminutive witch!” The voice was distant thunder, remarkably polite. “I am Ignis, and I sense a need for haste! Shall I incinerate this bridge? A single magnificent gout of flame, and you’ll be across faster than a streaking comet!”

Pepper’s growl was small and entire. Brindle’s palms prickled. Incinerate. She pictured the bridge gone, the parcel scorched, her careful boots with nowhere to be careful.

Ignis offered, next, to carry them at breakneck speed, or to leap the whole valley in one theatrical bound. The spectacle tugged at her. It would be a story. It would also be a very good way to miss a buckle.

“No, thank you, Ignis. This bridge will suffice. With care.”

Ignis looked faintly disappointed, as if she had refused a fireworks display. He settled on a crag instead, a courteous mountain of emerald, and watched. Brindle went on placing boots. Pepper went on being a small black certainty against her shawl. The planks complained. The mist made silver beads on the ropes. Halfway across, a fungus the colour of old coins caught her eye, and she nearly stopped to ask it a scholarly question. The satchel bumped her hip. She did not stop.

They reached the hermitage, a stone dwelling that clung to the mountain like a determined goat. Wizard Cedric opened the door. His beard was spun silver. His eyes twinkled as if they had been collecting knowledge for a inconveniently long time.

“Ah, the heartstone. Excellent, Brindle. Just in time.”

He opened the satchel and began to fit the Sunstone mechanism. Then a crease appeared between his brows.

“Wait. Where is the little pebble? The one that fits the casing, like a moonbeam caught in a dewdrop?”

Brindle’s stomach dropped. She scanned satchel, pockets, cuffs. A small grey unassuming pebble, worn smooth — the kind you would barely notice on a path. The very pebble she had used that morning to prop open her cottage door, so the breeze would not swing it shut on her carefully arranged displays.

“Oh, dear.”

The moon had already begun its descent, long shadows dragging down the slopes. Retracing the bridges would take too long. Asking Ignis meant handing her quiet competence to a creature who wanted colossal magnifying lenses and concentrated moonlight. She stood on the hermitage ledge with Pepper warm against her wrist and the valley dark below, and for a moment she wanted only her hearthstone and her aligned jars. The wind found a mournful note in the cliff. Cedric waited without hurrying her. Pride sat in her hands like a bird that did not wish to be put down.

She called anyway.

“Ignis! I require your assistance. A small pebble. A very important small pebble. Near my cottage door.”

Ignis, who had been admiring his reflection in a waterfall with great enthusiasm, swooped down with a delighted roar.

“A pebble! This calls for a truly colossal magnifying lens! Or a carefully aimed beam of concentrated moonlight! I have just the spell!”

Brindle held up a hand. “No. Just a very gentle lift. From my cottage door. It is crucial it not be disturbed.”

They flew. Brindle and Pepper perched on Ignis’s broad warm back. The wind whipped her hair into a weather of its own. For all his dramatic inclinations, the dragon kept a steady, careful rhythm, wings beating like a huge calm clock. Cottage-light appeared below, her own windows, her own door still propped by that ridiculous grey pebble. He landed with a soft puff of displaced air and, with a delicate flick of his colossal snout, nudged the pebble free of the worn wood. Pepper inspected the snout, found it acceptable, and sat down as if this had always been the plan. Then Ignis carried the pebble back as if the mountain itself had asked him to be precise.

Cedric fitted the pebble. The mechanism hummed. The heartstone pulsed. The Sunstone bathed the valley in warm gold just as the moon touched the western horizon, orange and purple stacked along the peaks. Brindle’s knees remembered they had been locked.

Later, her cottage smelled of roasted pine nuts and something faintly exotic — Ignis’s mountain spices, presented with a flourish that involved a cascade of glittering dust and very nearly toppled a bundle of thyme. He told stories of his youth, punctuated by gestures that made Pepper bat at stray embers. Ignis, with a wink, puffed a tiny dancing flame that mimicked a firefly. Brindle did not restack the herbs until he had finished.

When he boomed a farewell, promising to personally escort any future errant pebbles across the cosmos, she watched him become a slightly over-the-top silhouette against the stars. She picked up a fallen pinecone from the hearth. Rough. Ordinary. No grand magic in it.

Pepper climbed into her lap and purred as if the jars had been this slightly crooked all along. Brindle left them crooked, and set the pebble — a spare, this time — in a dish where she could see it, instead of under the door.
characters: Brindle (a witch), Pepper (a cat), Cedric (a wizard)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
author: StoryGen Community
